READING

**The financial arithmetic**

The all-in capital comparison is:

| | VELLACOTT | TARNSIDE |
|---|---|---|
| Vessel | £3,050,000 | £1,420,000 |
| Linkspan / charter | £240,000 | £310,000 |
| Less Brindlemere sale | −£610,000 | — |
| **Total outlay** | **£2,680,000** | **£1,730,000** |

VELLACOTT costs £950,000 more upfront. At £190,000 a year in fuel savings the payback period on that extra outlay is exactly five years, reaching break-even around the end of the 2031 summer season. After that every year runs £190,000 cheaper than TARNSIDE would.

That five-year payback is, on its own, a strong argument. But it is not the decisive one.

**The hull arithmetic**

TARNSIDE is not just a decision to re-engine; it is a decision to carry a 1995 hull through the 2030s. Even with new machinery she will be a 37-year-old vessel by the time the fuel savings under VELLACOTT have repaid the capital difference, and she will need replacing sometime in the decade after that. When that day comes, Cormorant Sound Ferries pays a second large capital bill — and in the meantime it has been paying the £190,000 annual fuel premium throughout. TARNSIDE does not avoid the vessel-replacement problem; it defers it by perhaps ten to fifteen years while paying more to run the service.

The Suilvenaig at nine years old is at the beginning of her productive life. A well-maintained small RoPax hull of this generation should give twenty-five or more years of service from handover, meaning the next equivalent capital decision falls in the early 2050s rather than the late 2030s.

When you fold the deferred-replacement cost into the analysis, VELLACOTT is substantially cheaper over the realistic life of either asset, not just marginally better.

**The complications of VELLACOTT, taken seriously**

*Masters.* Losing two of nine is a real operational stress on a year-round single-vessel service. Seven masters is workable — eleven crossings a day on a single vessel needs two shifts at most — but the rota margin shrinks and illness cover becomes tighter. The six-week endorsement course needs to be started immediately for the remaining seven, probably running two masters through sequentially so that at least two or three are qualified before the Suilvenaig arrives on 20 November. The two retirements are an accelerated version of an inevitable transition; the question is whether they can recruit a replacement master over the following season to restore rota depth. That is a planning task, not a reason to reject the course.

*Insurance.* The broker has not yet quoted. For a nine-year hull versus a thirty-one-year hull with original engines, the outcome is unlikely to be worse; it may well be better. This uncertainty should be resolved before contracts are signed, not used as grounds to stay with TARNSIDE.

*Linkspan.* £240,000, and it must be complete before the Suilvenaig can operate. Twelve to thirteen weeks from now to the handover date is tight for a marine civil works package. This needs to be contracted and started immediately.

*Brindlemere sale.* The Kittiwake valuation of £610,000 holds until 11 February 2027. The operational sequence must be: Suilvenaig delivered, linkspan complete, at least two masters endorsed, Suilvenaig in service — then sell the Brindlemere. She should not be sold until the replacement is actually running. The February deadline is enough time to manage this if VELLACOTT is approved promptly.

**The complications of TARNSIDE, taken seriously**

The twelve-week yard period falls January to April 2027, which is the winter schedule (five crossings a day). That is the best possible time for disruption. The charter at £310,000 has been agreed in principle. This is the strongest operational argument for TARNSIDE: the disruption is bounded, planned and covered.

The weaker side of TARNSIDE is that it resolves nothing structurally. The engines get replaced; everything else stays the same. The hull continues to age, the fuel bill continues to be £190,000 a year worse, and the vessel-replacement problem is simply handed to a future management team.

**Summary of the balance**

VELLACOTT asks for £950,000 more upfront, requires immediate action on masters, insurance, linkspan and the sale sequence, and involves losing two experienced masters. These are genuine complications. None of them is a blocker if managed promptly.

TARNSIDE asks for £950,000 less upfront and carries far less immediate operational complexity. Its cost is paid over time: in fuel, in the certainty of a further large capital call within fifteen years, and in the continuing depreciation of a thirty-one-year hull.

On a five-year view TARNSIDE is defensible. On any longer view VELLACOTT is clearly better value. For a company holding a year-round statutory licence with a single-vessel operation, the younger hull is also the lower long-term risk.

The deciding condition: get the insurance quote before exchanging on the Suilvenaig, and begin master endorsement training this week.

---

READING
  The fuel saving of £190,000 a year recoups the £950,000 additional outlay within five years, and beyond that point VELLACOTT also defers the next full vessel-replacement event by roughly fifteen years relative to TARNSIDE, making the higher upfront spend the cheaper outcome over the realistic service life of either asset. The operational complications — master rota reduction, linkspan timing, insurance unknown — are real but each is manageable with prompt action, whereas TARNSIDE's apparent simplicity is purchased by paying more annually and guaranteeing a second capital crisis within the planning horizon.

CALL
  VELLACOTT

GROUNDS
  The five-year fuel-saving payback on the extra £950,000 is compelling in itself, but the decisive point is that TARNSIDE merely defers a second large vessel-replacement programme by a decade or so while paying £190,000 a year more in the meantime, whereas VELLACOTT's nine-year hull settles that question for a generation.
